Normal: No ready TPM. If this PC has one, enable it in the BIOS/UEFI (look for 'TPM', 'PTT' on Intel, or 'fTPM' on AMD).
Without a TPM you cannot run Windows 11 and drive encryption is weaker.

Secure Boot is off, so tampered boot code would not be blocked. Enable it in BIOS/UEFI — but note that switching a system installed in legacy BIOS mode requires converting the disk first (MBR2GPT), so research before changing it.
This drive is not encrypted: anyone who removes it can read every file, no password needed. That matters most for laptops and any PC that leaves your home.
Turn on BitLocker (Pro editions) or Device Encryption (Home) — and SAVE THE RECOVERY KEY somewhere outside this PC before you start.

rules.forecast: Unencrypted drives are the most common way personal data is stolen from lost or discarded computers.

Bad: Nothing is backing up your personal files. Set up a backup today — this is the single most valuable thing on this whole report.
Simplest option: plug in an external drive and turn on File History (Control Panel > File History), or turn on OneDrive folder backup for Desktop/Documents/Pictures.
Aim for the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of anything you care about, on 2 different kinds of media, with 1 copy kept off-site or in the cloud.

rules.forecast: Every drive eventually fails, and ransomware targets whatever it can reach. A backup is the only defence that works after the fact.

Normal: No system restore points exist, so you cannot roll back a bad driver or update. Turn on System Protection for the Windows drive (Control Panel > System > System Protection) and create one now.
Restore points protect Windows settings — they do NOT back up your documents.
Your newest restore point is old. Create a fresh one before installing drivers or major updates (search 'Create a restore point' in Start).
File History is off. With an external drive connected, it keeps automatic versioned copies of your libraries — the easiest real backup on Windows (Control Panel > File History).
